1 Executive Summary
This document is the fifth in a series of technical analyses for the Dolphin PCIe Fabric project.
Previous documents include: (1) Literature Review, (2) Architectural Design, (3) Performance
Analysis, and (4) Security Analysis. This Market Expansion Plan builds on those foundations to
chart the path to commercial deployment.
The centralized cloud model is economically and environmentally unsustainable. Consumers
pay $10-20/month for storage they could host locally for pennies of electricity, while data centers
consume 20 GW of US power to serve workloads that are 30-50% edge-suitable. Meanwhile, billions
of dollars of idle compute capacity sits in home PCs during off-hours, and ISPs struggle with last-
mile bandwidth congestion.
Our three-node PCIe fabric prototype demonstrates a fundamentally different architecture:
router-resident storage accessible at microsecond latency via Dolphin’s SISCI API, enabling
always-available community cloud infrastructure without traditional data center overhead. By
extending PCIe fabric across fiber-optic links between homes, we create a neighborhood-scale virtual
data center where storage, memory, and compute resources are pooled and shared with datacenter-
class performance.
This plan charts the path from prototype to commercial deployment, addressing the critical
questions: How do we scale from 3 nodes to 100+ homes? Who pays for it? How do we harden
security from 37% to 95%? How do we reduce cost from $4,175 to $800 per home? The answer lies
in strategic ISP partnerships, parallel development to compress timelines, and manufacturing scale
to drive down costs.
1.1 Key Value Propositions
• For Consumers: 24/7 storage availability without keeping PCs powered; 100×lower la-
tency than cloud; privacy through local ownership; passive income via device lending ($10-
50/month)
• For ISPs: 40-60% backbone bandwidth reduction (saves $10k-100k/year per 1,000 homes);
new premium tier revenue ($50-70/subscriber/month)
• For Institutional Buyers: 50-90% cost reduction vs. cloud storage for edge-appropriate
workloads; sub-millisecond latency for CAD/ML/medical imaging

3 Smart Router Architecture
The “smart router” is a network appliance that combines traditional routing with 2-8 TB NVMe
storage, PCIe fabric adapter, and compute capability. It stays powered 24/7 (unlike PCs), provides
always-available storage, and coordinates device lending across the neighborhood mesh.
3.1 Core Design
Hardware Specification:
• CPU: ARM/x86 (8+ cores, 65W TDP) - $280
• RAM: 32 GB DDR4 ECC - $120
• Storage: 2-8 TB NVMe Gen4 - $180-720
• PCIe Fabric: Dolphin MXH930 (4-port Gen4) - $1,200 → $840 at volume
• Fiber Conversion: Samtec PCIEAOC (10m-10km, <500ns latency) - $400-800/link
• Security: TPM 2.0 chip - $25
• Target BOM: $1,980 (Phase 2 volume pricing)
3.2 Three-Tier Memory Hierarchy
1. Tier 1 (DRAM Cache): 16-32 GB volatile cache for hot data; LRU eviction; synced via
reflective memory (hardware-coherent cache shared across nodes)
2. Tier 2 (Router NVMe): 2-8 TB persistent storage; distributed RAID-6 (8+2 erasure
coding = 8 data chunks + 2 parity chunks, allowing any 2 routers to fail without data loss);
1.25×overhead means 1 TB usable requires 1.25 TB raw storage
3. Tier 3 (Remote Router NVMe): Multi-hop access for cold storage; <10 µs cross-
neighborhood latency
3.3 Device Lending and Wake-on-PCIe
Device lending allows idle GPUs/CPUs in sleeping PCs to be rented to neighbors. The router wakes
the PC remotely, makes the device accessible over PCIe fabric as if locally installed, and credits the
owner’s account.
Protocol:
1. Broker receives GPU/CPU request → queries DHT for idle resources
2. Send SISCI interrupt + Ethernet WoL → target PC boots minimal Linux (5-15 sec)
3. Export GPU BAR as SISCI segment → requester maps as local PCIe device
6

4. Workload completes → PC returns to sleep → credit owner account
Economics: $0.50-2 per GPU-hour (competitive with AWS spot instances)
3.4 Inter-Home Fiber Connectivity
Samtec Solution: PCIEAOC series active optical cables
• Range: 10m-300m (multimode OM4), 1km-10km (single-mode OS2)
• Compatibility: Drop-in replacement for copper; transparent to SISCI driver
• Cost: $400-800 per 100m link (Phase 2); $200-400 at Phase 3 volume
• Installation: Professional fiber pull ($5-15/meter) or DIY for adjacent homes

4.2 Device Lending Security

5 Scaling Roadmap
Deployment scales from single-home (intra-home PC connections) to neighborhood (10-20 homes
via fiber) to regional (100-1,000 homes with ISP aggregation nodes). Each phase reduces cost,
increases performance, and adds security hardening.
5.1 Phase 1: Single-Home Mesh (Months 1-6)
Topology: Router + 2-4 client PCs (intra-home, copper cables <5m)
Key Deliverables:
• Router firmware with token auth, AppArmor, IOMMU isolation
• FUSE-based distributed file system (metadata in reflective memory)
• Web UI (dashboard, topology viewer, device lending config)
• 10 alpha units deployed to beta testers
Cost: $4,175/home (DIY prototype pricing)
5.2 Phase 2: Neighborhood Mesh (Months 7-18)
Topology: 10-20 homes, partial mesh via Samtec fiber (star + ring hybrid)
Key Deliverables:
• Multi-hop DMA routing (>80% throughput at 2 hops)
• Distributed RAID-6 (Reed-Solomon 8+2 = files split into 8 data chunks + 2 parity chunks
distributed across 10 routers; any 2 routers can fail simultaneously without data loss)
• AES-256-GCM encryption (throughput drops to 10.5 GB/s)
• ISP pilot deployment (20-50 homes)
Cost: $2,640/home (37% reduction via volume discounts)

6 Router Software Stack (High-Level Architecture)
The smart router runs a custom Linux distribution with six software layers: base OS with drivers,
fabric management daemons, distributed storage services, user interfaces, monitoring/telemetry,
and standard networking. No actual code is shown - this is architectural overview only.
6.1 Six Layers
1. Base Operating System: Custom Linux Mint fork (“DolphinOS”), kernel 6.8+ with Soft-
ware Infrastructure for Shared-Memory Cluster Interconnect (SISCI) driver, Linux Unified
Key Setup (LUKS)-encrypted B-tree File System (BTRFS)
2. Fabric Management: Discovery daemon, authentication token daemon, rate limiter/Quality
of Service (QoS), device lending broker
3. Storage/Caching: Reflective memory cache manager, distributed file system (FS, POSIX-
compatible), Redundant Array of Independent Disks (RAID) rebuild daemon
4. User Interfaces / Application Programming Interfaces: React web user interface (UI),
Representational State Transfer (REST) API, iOS/Android applications (React Native)
5. Monitoring: Prometheus metrics exporter, extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) audit
consumer, remote system logger (rsyslog) + optional Elasticsearch-Logstash-Kibana (ELK)
stack
6. Routing: Standard Network Address Translation (NAT)/firewall (iptables), Dynamic Host
Configuration Protocol (DHCP, dnsmasq), Domain Name System (DNS, Unbound), optional
SuperSockets proxy

8 Market Opportunities
Total addressable market is $25B US, $75B globally, split across consumer (home enthusiasts, cre-
ators), small business (offices, studios), and institutional (universities, ML startups). Prioritization
favors early adopters with technical sophistication and budget.
8.1 Market Landscape and Opportunity
The market for edge computing infrastructure sits at the intersection of three powerful trends:
cloud repatriation (businesses moving workloads back from AWS/Azure), the creator economy’s
demand for high-performance local storage, and institutional buyers seeking alternatives to expen-
sive proprietary solutions. Together, these segments represent a $25B domestic opportunity and
$75B globally.
The consumer segment ($15B) is anchored by technically sophisticated early adopters. Home lab
enthusiasts—5 to 10 million US households with disposable income and willingness to pay $2,000-
4,000 for premium infrastructure—represent our beachhead. The r/DataHoarder community alone
exceeds 800,000 subscribers, demonstrating both market size and organic evangelism potential.
Content creators (5M US) face a similar pain point: 4K and 8K video workflows demand fast local
storage, but cloud sync is prohibitively expensive at scale. These users already budget $2,000-3,000
for production equipment and understand the value proposition immediately. Remote workers (15-
20M US) round out the consumer opportunity, particularly when employers subsidize home office
infrastructure.

Small business ($5B) adoption follows consumer proof-of-concept. Six million small offices
nationwide currently pay $500-2,000 monthly for cloud storage and backup—annual fees that dwarf
a one-time $3,000-5,000 router investment. Video production studios (10,000 US) face even sharper
economics: our $10,000-20,000 solution replaces $50,000+ fiber channel SANs while delivering
comparable performance. The payback period for these segments is measured in months, not
years.
Institutional buyers ($5B) represent Phase 3 expansion after consumer/SMB validation. Univer-
sity STEM departments (4,000 programs nationwide) operate on grant funding cycles and regularly
allocate $50,000-200,000 for departmental HPC infrastructure. Machine learning startups (50,000
US) burn $2-5 per GPU-hour on AWS; a shared neighborhood GPU lending pool offers 50-70%
cost reduction while maintaining comparable access. These buyers prioritize total cost of ownership
over upfront price, making them ideal candidates once the platform matures.
The total addressable market breaks down as $15B consumer, $5B small business, and $5B
institutional domestically, with global markets approximately 3×larger. Our go-to-market strat-
egy prioritizes early adopters with technical sophistication and validated budgets, expanding to
mainstream segments as manufacturing scale reduces pricing.
9 ISP Partnership Strategy
ISPs are ideal go-to-market partners: they benefit from 40-60% backbone bandwidth reduction, can
fund pilots, handle fiber installation, and recruit neighborhoods. The strategy moves from pilot
(20-50 homes) to licensing/co-development at 1,000+ home scale.
9.1 The Strategic Case for ISP Partnership
Internet service providers are not merely a distribution channel—they are the natural strategic
partner for neighborhood-scale edge infrastructure. ISPs possess three critical assets we lack: fiber
installation capability, neighborhood customer relationships, and capital to fund pilots. In return,
they gain quantifiable backbone bandwidth savings, a differentiated premium tier offering, and a
hedge against edge computing competitors.
The economic case is straightforward. A typical neighborhood generates 500 GB per home per
month in backbone traffic—content streaming, cloud sync, video uploads, software updates. When
40% of this traffic is cached locally via PCIe fabric mesh, backbone demand drops to 6 TB/month
for a 20-home pilot, delivering $800-2,000 monthly savings in transit costs. Annualized, that’s
$9,600-24,000 in recurring savings against a $52,800 capital expenditure (20 routers at $2,640
each), yielding a 2.2 to 5.5 year payback. At 1,000-home scale, savings reach $40,000-100,000
annually—more than justifying a $600,000 pilot investment.
Our three-stage partnership playbook begins with an initial meeting targeting CTOs or VPs of
Network Engineering at regional ISPs (Sonic, Ting, Google Fiber) or national providers (AT&T,
Spectrum). The pitch focuses on immediate cost reduction: 40-60% backbone bandwidth savings
translating to $10,000-100,000 per year per 1,000 homes. We request $300,000-600,000 in pilot
funding for a 20-50 home deployment, positioning this as a low-risk proof-of-concept with clear
success metrics.
Stage two formalizes the pilot agreement within 4-6 months. The ISP commits pilot funding,
fiber installation labor, and neighborhood recruitment support. We deliver 20-50 production routers
with 12-month warranty and 24/7 monitoring dashboard. Success is measured quantitatively:
greater than 30% backbone reduction, customer satisfaction exceeding 4.0/5.0, uptime above 95%,

9.2 Target ISP Prioritization
Our prioritized target list balances technical sophistication, pilot budget availability, and strategic
fit. Sonic (150,000 California subscribers) leads due to tech-forward positioning and $300,000-
400,000 pilot budgets. Ting (30,000 multi-state subscribers) offers community focus and sim-
ilar budget. Google Fiber (2M subscribers) brings scale and existing edge compute interest
but requires $400,000-600,000 pilot investment. AT&T and Spectrum (5-7M fiber subscribers
each) represent long-term scale opportunities but face bureaucratic approval processes and demand
$600,000-1M pilot commitments. We approach regional ISPs first to establish proof points before
engaging nationals.
10 Data Center Impact
Edge computing can’t replace data centers, but can displace 30-50% of current workloads (personal
storage, caching, backup, dev/test). This saves 6 GW power, 30M tons CO2/year, and 540M
gallons/day water while reducing data center expansion pressure.
10.1 The Case for Workload Repatriation
Data centers are optimized for global-scale coordination, not personal file storage. When a consumer
pays Dropbox $12 per month for 2 TB of storage that sits idle 99% of the time, they’re subsidizing
datacenter real estate, redundant cooling, and backbone transit costs that dwarf the actual storage
value. This economic inefficiency scales poorly: US data centers now consume 20 GW of power
(2% of national electricity) to serve workloads that are 30-50% edge-suitable.
We categorize datacenter workloads by locality of reference and tolerance for moderate latency.
Edge-suitable workloads share three characteristics: they serve a small geographic footprint,
tolerate 1-10 millisecond latency, and benefit from data gravity near users. Personal cloud stor-
age (Dropbox, Google Drive) is 100% edge-suitable—files are overwhelmingly accessed by their
owner from predictable locations. Content caching (Netflix, YouTube edge nodes) is 80% re-
placeable since 80% of views concentrate in popular content that can be pre-positioned. Backup
and archival services (Backblaze, Carbonite) are 90% edge-suitable as restores are infrequent and
latency-insensitive. Development and test environments (EC2/Azure staging) achieve 70% edge-
suitability since most dev/test traffic never leaves the organization. Batch processing workloads like
video transcoding and data analysis reach 60% edge-suitability when job duration exceeds network
transfer time.
Conversely, datacenter-resident workloads require global scale, extreme uptime, or regu-
latory compliance. Global-scale services (search engines, social media) must maintain single-digit
millisecond latency worldwide, necessitating datacenter deployment in dozens of regions. Mission-
critical high-availability services (banking, healthcare) demand 99.999% uptime (5 minutes annual

downtime) that edge infrastructure cannot guarantee. Compliance-driven workloads (PCI-DSS
payment processing, SOC2 audited services) face auditor requirements for physical security and
access logging that home routers cannot satisfy. Large-scale machine learning training requires
1,000+ GPU clusters with high-speed interconnect that exceeds neighborhood scale.
10.2 Quantified Environmental and Economic Impact
At full deployment across 10 million US homes (10% of broadband households), neighborhood-
scale edge infrastructure displaces measurable datacenter demand. Storage repatriation reaches
4.7 exabytes (47% of current US datacenter storage capacity), while compute offload captures
approximately 12% of datacenter compute cycles through device lending and batch processing.
The environmental impact is substantial. Power consumption decreases by 6 GW (30% of the
20 GW US datacenter load), translating to $6 billion annual electricity savings at commercial rates.
Carbon emissions drop by 30 million tons per year—equivalent to removing 6.5 million cars from
roads or negating the annual emissions of 3.5 million households. Water consumption for datacenter
cooling decreases by 540 million gallons daily, addressing a critical concern in drought-prone regions
like Arizona and Nevada where hyperscale datacenters face increasing public opposition.
We emphasize that this is not datacenter replacement but hybrid edge-cloud architecture.
Edge infrastructure handles local, personal, and latency-sensitive workloads while datacenters con-
tinue serving global coordination, mission-critical services, and compliance-driven applications. The
result is a more efficient allocation of compute resources: expensive datacenter capacity focuses on
workloads that genuinely require it, while commodity edge infrastructure serves the long tail of
personal and small-business use cases.
11 Parallel Development Strategy
Seven independent teams (hardware, kernel, services, UI, security, business development, QA)
working in parallel compress 36-month sequential timeline to 18 months. Total budget $7.39M
funded via seed round + Series A + ISP co-investment.

14 Appendices
14.1 A. Glossary
ASIC Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (custom silicon chip designed for a specific use, of-
fering higher performance and lower cost at scale than general-purpose chips)
PCIe Fabric High-speed interconnect that extends PCIe bus across multiple computers, allowing
direct memory access and device sharing as if components were in the same machine
15
Dolphin PCIe Fabric: Market Expansion Plan Version 2.0
SISCI Software Infrastructure for Shared-Memory Cluster Interconnect (Dolphin’s API)
DMA Direct Memory Access (zero-copy hardware transfer bypassing CPU)
Reflective Memory Hardware-synchronized cache where writes to one node automatically ap-
pear on all other nodes (like a distributed whiteboard)
Device Lending Remote access to idle GPUs/CPUs over PCIe fabric; sleeping PCs wake on
demand to provide compute resources for fee
RAID-6 / Erasure Coding Data protection scheme that splits files into chunks with parity
data, allowing reconstruction if any 2 storage nodes fail (8+2 = 8 data + 2 parity)
NTB Non-Transparent Bridge (PCIe topology for peer-to-peer)
AOC Active Optical Cable (PCIe-to-fiber conversion)
DHT Distributed Hash Table (peer discovery protocol)
IOMMU Input-Output Memory Management Unit (DMA isolation for security)
TPM Trusted Platform Module (hardware security chip for encryption keys)
EAL2 Common Criteria Evaluation Assurance Level 2 (security certification)
